transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: The city of Amsterdam in the Netherlands has announced an ambitious new plan to become completely circular in its construction industry by 2040. The initiative requires that all new buildings and major renovation projects use at least 25 percent recycled or reused materials by 2030, increasing to 100 percent circularity by 2040. City officials estimate that the construction sector currently produces around 40 percent of the city's waste and accounts for a significant portion of carbon emissions. Under the new policy, builders will be required to submit material passports for every new project, documenting the origin, composition, and potential for future reuse of all building materials. The city is also creating a digital marketplace where construction companies can buy and sell used materials, reducing waste and lowering costs. Several pilot projects have already demonstrated success, including a recently completed apartment complex built almost entirely from reused bricks, steel beams, and windows salvaged from demolished buildings. City leaders hope the initiative will not only reduce environmental impact but also create new jobs in material recovery and sustainable construction.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard. (British Female)

2. What is a material passport?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Male)
paras: A new archaeological discovery in Egypt has revealed a 3,000-year-old lost city near Luxor that is being described as one of the most important finds since the discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb. Archaeologists from a team led by renowned Egyptologist Dr. Zahi Hawass uncovered the city, which dates back to the reign of King Amenhotep III, one of Egypt's most powerful pharaohs. The site includes well-preserved houses, bakeries, workshops, and administrative buildings, with many everyday objects still in place, offering unprecedented insight into daily life during ancient Egypt's golden age. Excavations began last year after archaeologists found stone inscriptions pointing to the city's location. The team has already uncovered jewelry, pottery, and even mud bricks stamped with the pharaoh's official seal. Researchers say the city appears to have been abandoned relatively suddenly, possibly during a relocation of the royal capital, which helped preserve many artifacts in excellent condition. The discovery is expected to keep archaeologists busy for at least a decade as they carefully excavate and analyze the site.
Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard. (British Female)

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: A major consumer electronics company has unveiled new accessibility features for its smartphones that will allow people with disabilities to control their devices entirely through eye movements and voice commands. The technology, which uses advanced artificial intelligence and the phone's front-facing camera to track eye gaze accurately, enables users to navigate menus, type messages, browse the internet, and use apps without touching the screen. For people with motor impairments caused by conditions such as spinal cord injuries, multiple sclerosis, or cerebral palsy, this technology could dramatically increase independence and access to digital services. The company worked closely with disability advocates and people with disabilities throughout the development process to ensure the features are practical and intuitive. In addition to eye tracking, the update includes improved voice recognition that better understands speech patterns of people with various speech impairments, as well as new hearing aid compatibility features. The accessibility features will be available as a free software update for all recent models starting next month. Accessibility organizations have praised the announcement, noting that technology has the potential to remove barriers but only if companies prioritize inclusive design from the beginning.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Claire): Excuse me, could you help me? I'm trying to return this sweater I bought last week, but I can't find my receipt.
Man (Store Clerk): Of course, I can help you with that. Do you remember approximately when you purchased it, and did you use a credit card or a store account?

Woman: It was last Tuesday, so exactly a week ago. And I used my Visa card—I think the last four digits are 4455. I have the tags still attached, and I haven't worn it at all. I just realized when I got home that the color doesn't really match anything else I own.

Man: No problem at all. Let me look up your transaction... Yes, here it is, from last Tuesday afternoon—one wool sweater in forest green, 68 dollars. Because you don't have the physical receipt, I can't give you a cash refund, but I can offer you either an exchange for a different color or item, or store credit that you can use anytime.
Woman: Oh, store credit would be perfect actually. I saw a nice scarf on the sale rack that I might like more anyway. How does store credit work? Do I get a gift card?

Man: I can put the full 68 dollars onto a store gift card for you right now. It never expires, and you can use it at any of our locations nationwide. If you want to look around and pick out the scarf now, I can process both transactions at once. Otherwise, you can just take the card and come back another time.
Woman: Let me take a quick look at the accessories section and see if that scarf is still there. I'll be right back in just a minute.

Man: Take your time. I'll have the return paperwork started while you browse. Also, just so you know, all sale items are final sale, but you'll still have our usual 30-day return policy on anything you buy at regular price using the store credit.
Woman: Good to know, thank you so much for your help. I really appreciate it.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard. (British Female)

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Female + British Male)
paras: Man (Ben): Hi Olivia, have you decided where you're going for summer break this year?

Woman (Olivia): Hey Ben! I'm actually planning a road trip with my sister. We're thinking of driving up the Pacific Coast Highway, starting in Los Angeles and going all the way up to Seattle. We have about two weeks, so we want to take our time and stop at lots of places along the way.
Man: That sounds incredible! I did a similar trip a couple of years ago, and it's one of the most beautiful drives I've ever done. Do you have a rough itinerary planned yet?

Woman: Not really, that's why I wanted to ask you—what were your favorite stops? We definitely want to see Big Sur, and we're planning to spend a couple of days in San Francisco, but we're not sure what else is worth stopping for between LA and San Francisco, and then from SF up to Seattle.

Man: Big Sur is absolutely amazing—make sure you stop at Bixby Creek Bridge, it's the most photographed bridge in California for a reason. Between LA and SF, I really loved Santa Barbara—it's a beautiful coastal town with great restaurants. And San Luis Obispo is a cute college town with a nice downtown area. North of SF, you absolutely have to go to Redwood National Park to see the giant trees. They're impossible to describe—pictures don't do them justice. And then in Oregon, Cannon Beach is stunning with those big rock formations in the water.
Woman: That all sounds perfect. How far in advance do you think we should book accommodation? I've heard some of the national park lodges fill up months ahead.

Man: Yeah, if you want to stay inside Redwood National Park, you should book that pretty soon—like now. For motels and hotels in towns, you can probably wait a few weeks, but since it's summer peak season, I wouldn't wait too long. Camping is also a great option if you're into that—many state parks have nice campgrounds right on the coast.
Woman: We were actually thinking of renting a camper van to save money on accommodation and have more flexibility. Do you have any experience with that?

Man: I did that on my trip! It was great waking up right by the ocean. Just make sure you book the camper van early too, because they get reserved quickly in summer. And check if there are any restrictions on where you can park overnight—some towns don't allow sleeping in vehicles.
Woman: That's really helpful advice. Thanks so much, Ben! I'll start making reservations this weekend.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: Social media has become an integral part of modern life, with billions of people around the world using platforms like Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and TikTok to connect with friends, share content, and stay informed. While these platforms offer undeniable benefits—including staying in touch with distant family members, organizing community events, and providing a platform for underrepresented voices—research has increasingly raised concerns about the impact of excessive social media use on mental health, particularly among teenagers and young adults. Multiple studies have found a correlation between heavy social media use—defined as more than three hours per day—and increased rates of anxiety, depression, loneliness, and low self-esteem, especially in adolescent girls. Several factors contribute to these negative outcomes. One major issue is social comparison: people typically share their most positive moments and carefully curated images online, which can lead others to feel that their own lives are inadequate in comparison. Cyberbullying is another significant problem, with harmful comments and harassment following young people from school into their homes through their devices. Social media can also be highly addictive, with algorithmic feeds designed to keep users scrolling for as long as possible, often at the expense of sleep, homework, and in-person social interactions. However, experts emphasize that social media is not inherently harmful, and moderate use can be healthy. They recommend setting screen time limits, being mindful of how content makes you feel while using it, and making time for offline activities and face-to-face relationships. Many platforms have also begun introducing tools to help users monitor and limit their usage.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: The Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain in the late 18th century and spread throughout Europe and North America over the next hundred years, marked one of the most profound transformations in human history. Before industrialization, most people lived in rural communities and worked in agriculture, producing goods by hand in small workshops or cottages. The invention of steam power, mechanized textile production, and new iron-making processes fundamentally changed how goods were manufactured, leading to the rise of factories and mass production. This shift brought about massive social and economic changes. Millions of people moved from countryside to cities to work in factories, leading to rapid urbanization and the growth of industrial cities like Manchester, Birmingham, and Pittsburgh. While industrialization eventually raised living standards for many, the early factory system was notorious for harsh working conditions: long hours, low pay, dangerous machinery, and widespread child labor. Workers had few rights or protections, and labor unions gradually formed to advocate for better conditions, higher wages, and shorter workdays. The Industrial Revolution also transformed transportation with the development of steam-powered locomotives, railroads, and steamships, making it faster and cheaper to move goods and people across long distances. Environmental consequences became apparent early as well, with factory smoke polluting air and water in industrial cities—a pattern that would repeat globally as industrialization spread. The changes set in motion during this period created the modern industrialized world, shaping everything from work patterns and social structures to global economics and environmental challenges we still face today.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Volunteering—donating time and energy to help others without financial compensation—benefits not only the recipients of help but also the volunteers themselves in significant and often surprising ways. While most people volunteer first and foremost to contribute to their communities or support a cause they care about, research consistently shows that volunteering provides substantial physical and mental health benefits for people of all ages. One comprehensive study from the London School of Economics found that people who volunteered regularly reported higher levels of life satisfaction and lower rates of depression compared to non-volunteers, even after controlling for factors like income and overall health. For older adults, volunteering has been linked to lower blood pressure, reduced risk of cognitive decline, and even longer lifespan. Researchers believe these health benefits come from several sources: volunteering increases social connection, reducing isolation and loneliness; it provides a sense of purpose and meaning; and it often involves physical activity, whether that's building houses, cleaning up parks, or walking dogs at an animal shelter. Young people who volunteer also gain important benefits, including developing practical skills, building professional networks, and gaining work experience that can improve their college applications and future employment prospects. Many high schools now require community service hours for graduation, recognizing that volunteering helps build civic responsibility and empathy alongside practical skills. Volunteering comes in countless forms, from formal positions with nonprofit organizations to informal help for neighbors and community members. The key is finding an opportunity that matches your interests and schedule, whether that means tutoring children after school, serving meals at a homeless shelter, helping with disaster relief, or simply checking in on elderly neighbors regularly.
